title: When a Return May Still Be Raised on a Northbeam Returns and Restocking Schedule
content:
A return is raised only when the customer asks within the return window of the schedule the line falls under, counted from the day the item was delivered or collected. The return window is counted in calendar days from the anchor day, which counts as day zero, and the grace hours the schedule allows are added to the end of the last day. The anchor is what the schedule's anchor basis names, and where the item was collected in store the collection day is the delivery day; a line never yet delivered is cancelled on the order rather than returned. A line on a final sale schedule is not returned at all, and the only ground on which it comes back is that it arrived defective or was not what was described. Where the window has run out the return is refused and the customer is pointed to the protection plan on the item if one is in force, because a lapsed window is not a fault. A refusal may be appealed within the schedule's appeal window, and an appeal is decided on the same authorisation rather than by raising a new one.

## How the window is counted

The elements below are the elements of every Northbeam Returns and Restocking window.

| Element | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| The anchor | the day the item was delivered or collected, as the schedule's anchor basis names it; the collection day in store is the delivery day |
| Day zero | the anchor day itself |
| The count | calendar days from the anchor day |
| The length | the return window of the schedule the line falls under |
| After the last day | the grace hours the schedule allows, added to the end of the last day |
| The comparison | the day the customer asks must be not later than the end so counted |
| The boundary | the last day of the window satisfies it |

The condition is tested against the delivery day and the purchase day carried on the return authorisation record for that order line, not against the customer's recollection of when the item came, and it is tested before the return is raised. The authorisation compared is the one matched to the order line the customer is asking about.

## Boundary cases, on hypothetical facts

*A schedule whose window is the number of days published for it, an item delivered on the anchor day, and the customer asking on the last day of that window.* The anchor day counts as day zero, the last day is within the window, and the return is raised.

*The same schedule, the customer asking during the grace hours after the end of the last day.* Those hours are added to the end of the last day, so the request is still accepted at the counter.

*The same schedule, the customer asking after the grace hours have run.* The window has run out. The return is refused, and where a protection plan on the item is in force the customer is pointed to it, because a lapsed window is not a fault.

*An item on the order that has never been delivered.* There is no anchor day yet. The line is cancelled on the order rather than returned.

*A line on a final sale schedule.* It is not returned at all. The only ground on which it comes back is that it arrived defective or was not what was described.
